JSON: Name: refa_continuous_compliance_pipeline Title: Longitudinal empirical evaluation of an artefact-centric reference architecture and assessment protocol for continuous security compliance in DevOps Short Hypothesis: Using an artefact-centric reference architecture together with a structured assessment protocol (RefA + RefA-AP) causes a statistically significant increase in the per-sprint remediation rate of IEC 62443-4-1 compliance gaps and a reduction in mean time-to-remediate, relative to activity-based or business-as-usual assessment practices. Related Work: Prior work includes activity-based security-assessment frameworks and DevSecOps guidance that focus on prescribing security activities (for example, activity-centric audits, OWASP-SAMM-style program assessments, and tool-centric CI/CD security automation). Other contributions propose DevSecOps integration of threat modeling, secure coding, automated testing, and pipeline automation. Limitations of current approaches are: (1) weak grounding in certifiable industrial standards for product development (IEC 62443-4-1 specifically), (2) emphasis on activities rather than concrete artefacts as evidence, which hinders transferability to engineering teams and continuous assessment, (3) limited validation in regulated industrial DevOps contexts, and (4) lack of an end-to-end reporting and prioritization mechanism that supports sprint-level remediation and backlog integration. Existing maturity models typically measure organizational program maturity rather than per-pipeline artefact compliance and do not differentiate Dev vs Ops artefacts in CI/CD flows. Abstract: This research pipeline studies whether an artefact-centric Reference Architecture (RefA) and a paired assessment protocol (RefA-AP) enable continuous, sprint-level security compliance for DevOps teams operating under IEC 62443-4-1. The problem addressed is the tension between continuous DevOps delivery and the need to produce certifiable evidence of security-process compliance. We propose a structured empirical program: instantiate RefA and RefA-AP in multiple DevOps teams, collect artefact-level evidence across Plan–Monitor phases, and generate RefA-based maturity and improvement reports (RefA-AR) to drive backlog items. The main contribution is a validated evaluation pipeline that measures detection, remediation, and operational impact of artefact-centric continuous compliance versus activity-based baselines. Expected outcomes are quantified improvements in compliance-gap detection and remediation velocity, reproducible assessment artifacts mapped to IEC 62443-4-1, and an analysis of practical constraints for industrial adoption. Experiments: Datasets: 12–24 software-intensive DevOps projects across 3–6 industrial partners (IT/OT and cloud-native), each project providing CI/CD pipeline artifacts: build logs, SBOMs, SAST/DAST reports, code review records, deployment manifests, incident logs, and backlog items. Baselines: (A) Business-as-usual (ad-hoc / no structured assessment), (B) activity-based assessment (existing activity-centric checklist), (C) OWASP-SAMM-like maturity assessment. Treatment: RefA + RefA-AP + RefA-AR applied per sprint. Experimental design: mixed randomized matched-pairs and within-team pre/post design. Randomly assign comparable teams (matched by size, domain, maturity) to Baseline or Treatment for an initial 6-sprint trial; then perform cross-over or replication in additional teams. Metrics: primary—(1) remediation rate = number of IEC 62443-4-1 compliance gaps closed per sprint, (2) mean time-to-remediate (hours), (3) detection rate = number of unique compliance gaps detected per sprint; secondary—(4) assessor inter-rater agreement (Krippendorff’s alpha), (5) assessor effort (hours per assessment), (6) backlog integration latency (time from finding to backlog item creation), (7) precision/recall of artefact-to-standard mapping by automated parsers (if used). Baselines and treatment are compared using mixed-effects models with team and project as random effects; pre/post comparisons use paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests as appropriate. Ablation studies: (1) RefA full vs RefA without artefact view (practice-areas-only) to measure value of artefact-centric evidence; (2) RefA with manual assessment vs RefA augmented with automated artefact extraction (SBOM/SAST parsers) to measure automation impact. Additional analyses: subgroup analysis by project criticality (safety/critical vs non-critical) and by team security expertise. Sample size targets: power analysis to detect medium effect (Cohen’s d ~0.5) requires ~30 team-sprint units per condition; run for minimum 6 sprints per team. Data collection: standardized assessment spreadsheet (RefA-AQ), timestamped remediation events, and anonymized artefact evidence. Statistical significance threshold: p < 0.05, with correction for multiple comparisons. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) External validity: results may not generalize beyond projects that map to IEC 62443-4-1 contexts (IT/OT) or to organizations with mature DevOps tooling. 2) Confounding/team heterogeneity: differences in team maturity, prior security training, or product complexity may bias outcomes despite matching; mixed-effects models may not eliminate all confounders. 3) Measurement bias: manual assessments risk assessor subjectivity and inter-rater variability; automated parsers may yield false positives/negatives in artefact extraction. 4) Data access and confidentiality: industrial partners may limit access to raw artefacts, reducing dataset completeness or forcing aggregation that reduces analytic granularity. 5) Scalability and compute: automated analysis (SAST/SCA parsing at scale) may require significant compute and engineering effort; resource limits could constrain experiment size. 6) Ceiling/floor effects: teams already near compliance ceiling may show limited measurable improvement; conversely, very immature teams may require more than trial duration to show change. 7) Standard coverage limits: RefA ties to IEC 62443-4-1; gaps remain for operational cloud-native practices or other standards, limiting interpretation of outcomes across regulatory frameworks.
